stem: A nightly backup job reports 'completed successfully' every day. What MOST still needs to be verified before trusting recoverability?

options.text: That the backups can actually be restored via periodic restore tests
options.rationale: A completed backup is not proven usable until a restore test confirms the data can actually be recovered.

options.text: That the backup job has a colorful log
options.rationale: Log appearance is irrelevant to whether data can be restored.

options.text: That the server has a fast CPU
options.rationale: CPU speed does not confirm restorability of backups.

options.text: Nothing further; completion proves recoverability
options.rationale: Completion alone does not prove the backup is restorable; corruption or media faults can still prevent recovery.

stem: Which security process data source BEST reveals orphaned or dormant accounts?

options.text: Account management and access review data
options.rationale: Account/access review data reconciled against HR reveals accounts of departed users (orphaned) and unused (dormant) accounts.

options.text: The office thermostat log
options.rationale: Climate logs have nothing to do with account status.

options.text: The company lunch menu
options.rationale: This is irrelevant to account management.

options.text: The marketing campaign calendar
options.rationale: Marketing schedules do not reveal orphaned accounts.

stem: A company diligently collects extensive security metrics but no one reviews or acts on them. What is the MOST accurate assessment?

options.text: Collecting metrics provides little value unless they are reviewed by management and drive action
options.rationale: Metrics support decisions only when reviewed and acted upon; unreviewed data yields no improvement.

options.text: The metrics automatically fix the issues they measure
options.rationale: Metrics measure; they do not remediate on their own.

options.text: Collection alone guarantees compliance
options.rationale: Collection without review/action does not ensure compliance or improvement.

options.text: Unreviewed metrics are the ideal end state
options.rationale: Unreviewed metrics waste effort; review and action are the point.

stem: A rising rate of failed logins that may signal an emerging attack is MOST accurately which type of metric?

options.text: A Key Risk Indicator (KRI)
options.rationale: A KRI signals changing risk levels; a climbing failed-login rate is an early warning of elevated risk.

options.text: A Key Performance Indicator (KPI) of marketing
options.rationale: This is a risk signal, not a marketing performance metric.

options.text: A backup completion metric
options.rationale: Failed logins are unrelated to backup completion.

options.text: A physical badge count
options.rationale: Badge counts do not indicate login-based attack risk.

stem: Which data BEST measures the effectiveness of a security awareness program over time?

options.text: Trends in phishing-simulation click-rates and training completion
options.rationale: Declining click-rates and high completion, tracked over time, objectively indicate awareness-program effectiveness.

options.text: The number of posters printed
options.rationale: Producing materials is an output, not evidence of behavior change.

options.text: The cafeteria's daily specials
options.rationale: This is unrelated to awareness effectiveness.

options.text: The color of the training slides
options.rationale: Slide color does not measure effectiveness.

stem: Which characteristic MOST defines a useful security metric?

options.text: It is objective, relevant to objectives, and tracked over time
options.rationale: Good metrics are measurable/objective, tied to goals, and trended so change is visible.

options.text: It is subjective and changes definition each month
options.rationale: Subjective, inconsistent metrics cannot be compared or trended reliably.

options.text: It is collected once and never repeated
options.rationale: One-off metrics reveal no trend and limited insight.

options.text: It is unrelated to any security objective
options.rationale: Metrics disconnected from objectives provide little value.

stem: Tracking the percentage of systems patched within policy timelines MOST directly measures which process?

options.text: Patch/vulnerability management effectiveness
options.rationale: Patch-compliance rate shows how promptly systems are remediated, measuring the patch-management process.

options.text: Physical door security
options.rationale: Patch compliance is unrelated to physical doors.

options.text: Marketing reach
options.rationale: Patch metrics do not measure marketing.

options.text: Cafeteria throughput
options.rationale: This is irrelevant to patch management.

stem: Which collected data BEST indicates the organization's readiness to recover from a disaster?

options.text: Results and lessons learned from DR/BC exercises
options.rationale: DR/BC exercise outcomes reveal whether recovery plans actually work and where gaps remain.

options.text: The number of coffee cups used during the test
options.rationale: This trivia does not indicate recovery readiness.

options.text: The color of the DR runbook cover
options.rationale: Runbook aesthetics do not measure readiness.

options.text: The CEO's travel schedule
options.rationale: Executive travel is unrelated to DR readiness data.

stem: Mean Time To Detect (MTTD) and Mean Time To Respond (MTTR) are process data that MOST directly measure what?

options.text: The effectiveness of detection and incident response
options.rationale: MTTD/MTTR quantify how quickly incidents are detected and handled, measuring detection/response performance.

options.text: The speed of the office elevator
options.rationale: These metrics concern incident handling, not facilities.

options.text: The size of the marketing budget
options.rationale: Incident metrics are unrelated to marketing budgets.

options.text: The number of parking spaces
options.rationale: Parking is irrelevant to incident response metrics.

stem: What is the PRIMARY purpose of collecting security process data?

options.text: To provide objective evidence supporting management review, audit, and continuous improvement
options.rationale: Process data enables informed oversight, demonstrates control effectiveness to auditors, and drives improvement.

options.text: To fill storage with unused logs
options.rationale: Accumulating unused data is not the purpose; usable insight is.

options.text: To replace all security controls
options.rationale: Data measures controls; it does not replace them.

options.text: To eliminate the need for management
options.rationale: Data supports management decisions rather than removing management.

stem: To gain assurance that backups are usable, what should the team do FIRST beyond confirming job completion?

options.text: Perform periodic test restores of the backed-up data
options.rationale: Test restores verify the backup is actually recoverable, the essential validation beyond a completion status.

options.text: Delete the backups to free space
options.rationale: Deleting backups destroys the recovery capability being validated.

options.text: Assume completion equals recoverability
options.rationale: Completion does not guarantee a successful restore.

options.text: Stop backing up entirely
options.rationale: Stopping backups removes recovery capability.

stem: To keep account entitlement data accurate for oversight, what practice is BEST?

options.text: Conduct periodic access reviews and reconcile accounts with the HR authoritative source
options.rationale: Regular reviews reconciled to HR keep entitlement data current and surface anomalies like orphaned accounts.

options.text: Never review accounts once created
options.rationale: Unreviewed accounts drift and hide orphaned/excess access.

options.text: Let each user edit their own entitlements freely
options.rationale: Self-editing undermines oversight and least privilege.

options.text: Delete all account records to simplify
options.rationale: Deleting records removes the data needed for oversight.

stem: A Key Performance Indicator (KPI) in security primarily measures which of the following?

options.text: How well a security process is performing against its objectives
options.rationale: A KPI gauges performance of a process relative to defined objectives.

options.text: The color scheme of dashboards
options.rationale: Dashboard color is not a KPI.

options.text: The number of office plants
options.rationale: This is unrelated to security process performance.

options.text: The CEO's calendar density
options.rationale: Executive scheduling is not a security KPI.

stem: Why is tracking a security metric over time MOST valuable compared with a single snapshot?

options.text: Trends reveal whether the process is improving or degrading, informing action
options.rationale: Time-series data shows direction of change, enabling proactive decisions that a single number cannot.

options.text: A single number is always more actionable than a trend
options.rationale: A lone value lacks context; trends provide far more insight.

options.text: Trends make the data less accurate
options.rationale: Trending does not reduce accuracy; it adds context.

options.text: Snapshots eliminate the need for any metrics
options.rationale: Snapshots do not replace the value of ongoing measurement.

stem: Presenting a security scorecard to leadership for decisions MOST directly supports which activity?

options.text: Management review of security posture
options.rationale: A scorecard informs management review, enabling leadership to steer priorities and resources.

options.text: Fuzzing an application
options.rationale: Fuzzing is a testing technique, not a management review activity.

options.text: Physically shredding documents
options.rationale: Shredding is a disposal control, unrelated to management review of metrics.

options.text: Encrypting a hard drive
options.rationale: Disk encryption is a control, not the management-review activity.

stem: Manual metric gathering is inconsistent and slow. What is the BEST improvement?

options.text: Automate collection via SIEM/GRC dashboards for consistent, timely data
options.rationale: Automated tooling collects metrics consistently and promptly, reducing manual error and lag.

options.text: Stop collecting metrics entirely
options.rationale: Abandoning metrics removes oversight capability.

options.text: Collect metrics only once every few years
options.rationale: Rare collection provides no timely insight or trending.

options.text: Let each team invent its own untracked numbers
options.rationale: Inconsistent, untracked figures cannot be compared or trended.

stem: Using collected security data to iteratively refine controls in a plan-do-check-act manner MOST directly reflects which concept?

options.text: Continuous improvement
options.rationale: Feeding measurement back into refining controls is the essence of continuous improvement (PDCA).

options.text: Security through obscurity
options.rationale: Obscurity is unrelated to data-driven iterative improvement.

options.text: A denial-of-service attack
options.rationale: DoS is an attack, not an improvement process.

options.text: Key escrow
options.rationale: Key escrow is a key-management concept, unrelated to metric-driven improvement.

stem: If security metrics can be silently edited by the teams they measure, what is the MOST significant concern?

options.text: The integrity of the metrics is compromised, making them unreliable for oversight
options.rationale: Metrics that measured parties can alter cannot be trusted; integrity/segregation is needed for them to be meaningful evidence.

options.text: The metrics automatically become more accurate
options.rationale: Editable-by-the-measured metrics become less, not more, trustworthy.

options.text: It improves accountability
options.rationale: Self-editing reduces accountability and reliability.

options.text: There is no concern at all
options.rationale: Tamperable metrics are a serious integrity concern.

stem: An account with no login activity for 12 months is flagged in the account data. This MOST likely indicates what?

options.text: A dormant account that should be reviewed and possibly disabled
options.rationale: Long-unused accounts are dormant and increase risk; they should be reviewed and disabled if no longer needed.

options.text: A high-performing, well-used account
options.rationale: No activity for a year indicates disuse, not high use.

options.text: Proof of strong security
options.rationale: A lingering unused account is a risk, not evidence of strong security.

options.text: An account that must be given more privileges
options.rationale: Dormant accounts warrant review/disabling, not privilege increases.

stem: Which of the following is LEAST useful as security process data?

options.text: The brand of snacks in the vending machine
options.rationale: Vending-machine snacks provide no insight into security process performance, making it least useful.

options.text: Backup restore test results
options.rationale: Restore results are highly relevant to recoverability assurance.

options.text: Phishing-simulation click-rate trends
options.rationale: Click-rate trends measure awareness effectiveness.

options.text: Patch compliance rates
options.rationale: Patch rates measure remediation timeliness, useful process data.
